title: To Him we return
hookLine: those who, struck by loss, say we belong to Allah and to Him we return (2:156)
carry: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un

lines: A MESSAGE IN THE FAMILY CHAT.
THE SAME SHORT LINE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.
cards: A phone buzzes in a family group chat: someone's uncle has died. Within minutes the replies stack up, and if the family is Muslim, many are the same short Arabic line, typed in full or just the letters.
Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. Even people with little Arabic often know it. It's said at funerals, on hearing bad news, even when a phone screen cracks.
It comes from al-Baqarah, verse one hundred fifty-six. Today: to Him we return.

teach.b: Read the line where it sits. Just after remember Me comes a warning, not a comfort: God will surely test people with something of fear and hunger, and loss of wealth, lives and harvests.
Then: give good news to the patient, those who, when a calamity strikes them, say, in Pickthall's words: “Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning.” Two halves.

teach.h: WE BELONG TO GOD; WE RETURN TO HIM
teach.b: We belong to God: whatever was lost was never fully ours, and neither are we. And to Him we return: the loss isn't the end of the road.
The next verse says on such people are blessings from their Lord, and mercy, and they are the rightly guided. A hadith in Sahih Muslim shows what this did in one life.

Umm Salamah heard the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ teach that whoever is struck by a loss and says these words, adding, O God, reward me in my loss and give me something better in its place, will be given something better.
Then her husband, Abu Salamah, died.
She said the words, and wondered: who could be better than Abu Salamah, the first family to emigrate? She said them anyway. Later the Prophet himself asked to marry her.
In the hadith, she is the one telling the story.
And the line is spoken in the plural: we belong, we return. Even someone grieving alone says it as part of a we, which may be why it fits a family chat so well.

how: Muslims say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un on hearing of a death or any misfortune, and many add the supplication taught in Sahih Muslim asking God for reward in the loss and something better in its place.

o: the companion who said the words of return at her loss
the Prophet's daughter, who first recited the line
a poet whose elegy gave Muslims this line

games.q: the words of the patient — tap the pairs.
p: and to Him we are returning
fear, hunger, loss of wealth and lives
said it, and asked for something better

s: inna lillahi is only said when someone dies
Muslims say it at any loss or misfortune, large or small.
in al-Baqarah, the line comes right after a promise that people will be tested
fear, hunger, and loss of wealth, lives and harvests.
Umm Salamah thought no one could be better than her husband
she said the words anyway, as the hadith in Muslim tells.

games.q: you're Umm Salamah. your husband has died, and you've been taught to ask for something better in place of your loss. but who could be better than him?
o: skip the prayer; it can't be true.
games.why: she said it anyway. later the Prophet asked to marry her; the hadith in Muslim is her own telling.

practice: Bring to mind one loss, recent or old, large or small, and let yourself feel it for a moment without pushing it away.
Then, if you're Muslim or wish to, say the line slowly, inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un; if not, hold its two halves in English: this was never fully mine, and this isn't the end of the road.

wordCard.voice: Umm Salamah. The companion whose hadith teaches these words of return: say them even at the hardest loss, and trust what comes after. Today's word.

orig.say: IN-naa lil-LAA-hi wa IN-naa i-LAY-hi raa-ji-'OON
orig.note: Arabic: we belong to God, and to Him we are returning (2:156).

carryVoice: Your line: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. We belong to God, and to Him we return. Go gently.

sources.q: Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning.
